newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand outlines package to boost exports.
newsitem.headline: Thailand outlines package to boost exports.

text.p: Thailand said on Tuesday it would adopt a wide ranging tax and savings incentive package designed to boost export competitiveness and tackle its current account deficit problem.
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Amnuay Viravan told a news conference the cabinet approved package was designed to boost a slowing Thai economy.
He was commenting on the package which was approved by a cabinet panel chaired by him on August 30 and accepted by the full cabinet on Tuesday.

Under the package, which would be implemented gradually, Thailand would cut or lift tariffs on several dozen imported materials for food, textile, petrochemical, metal, and electronic products as well as auto spare parts, he said.
He said the government would speed up tax rebates, streamline tariff collection, and dismantle food import quota systems that he said contributed to high local food prices.
But the minister did not outline a time frame for implementing the package and gave scant details on related measures which need to be worked out by government agencies.
Market analysts said the package appeared to be a government response to criticism it had run out of ideas on how to cope with a rout in the Thai stock and currency markets.
"There is absolutely nothing new in this package which has been talked about many times in the past," said an analyst at broker Union Securities.
Amnuay said the government would promote Thailand's small commercial shipping fleet, offering Thai ship operators corporate tax exemptions as an incentive to modernise vessels.
He said the absence of a strong indegenous shipping fleet had caused much of Thailand's service account deficit.

To persuade Thai businessmen abroad to help narrow the current account deficit by repatriating profits back home, the government would ensure they were not subject to double taxation despite doing business in countries without tax treaties with Thailand.
Amnuay said Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa's coalition was determined to solve economic problems and reduce Thailand's short-term debt.
"The government would pursue fiscal and monetary policies to slow the rise of foreign debts even though they may be essential for national development."
Moody's Investors Service last week downgraded Thai ratings, saying a recent sharp rise in the country's short-term debt made it vulnerable to financial shocks through balance of payments.
Amnuay said the government would encourage long-term public savings by lifting a 15 percent withholding tax on up to 25,000 baht monthly bank savings.
